We show that there is an hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties of sets in a closed symplectic manifold: some sets cannot be displaced by symplectomorphisms from more sets than the others. We also find new examples of rigidity of intersections involving, in particular, specific fibers of moment maps of Hamiltonian torus actions, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds (following the works of P.Albers and P.Biran-O.Cornea), as well as certain, possibly singular, sets defined in terms of Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. In addition, we get some geometric obstructions to semi-simplicity of the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds. The proofs are based on the Floer-theoretical machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states.

We also identify new examples of intersection rigidity involving, in particular, specific fibers of moment maps associated with Hamiltonian torus actions; monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, building on the work of P. In addition, we obtain geometric obstructions to the semisimplicity of the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds. The proofs rely on the Floer-theoretic machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states.
outputs.L2: We establish a hierarchy of intersection-rigidity conditions for subsets of a closed symplectic manifold: certain subsets resist displacement by symplectomorphisms with respect to a broader collection of sets than others. We also provide new instances of rigid intersections, including particular fibers of moment maps arising from Hamiltonian torus actions, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds—building on work by P. Albers and by P. Biran and O. Cornea—and certain potentially singular subsets associated with Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. outputs.L3:
Subsets of a closed symplectic manifold can be organized according to a hierarchy of intersection rigidity: while some sets can be displaced from themselves by symplectomorphisms, others satisfy increasingly strong forms of nondisplaceability and must intersect their images under broad classes of symplectic transformations.

New examples of such rigid subsets arise among particular fibers of moment maps associated with Hamiltonian torus actions. Additional examples include certain monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, as well as potentially singular subsets defined using Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. Thus, the framework applies not only to smooth submanifolds but also to more general level sets and singular geometric objects.

These rigidity phenomena also have algebraic consequences. In particular, they yield geometric obstructions to the semisimplicity of the quantum homology of a symplectic manifold, revealing a direct connection between the intersection properties of subsets and the algebraic structure of quantum homology. The proofs are based on Floer-theoretic methods, especially the theory of partial symplectic quasi-states, which provides effective tools for detecting nondisplaceability and establishing stronger forms of symplectic rigidity.
outputs.L4:
This work develops a systematic hierarchy of intersection-rigidity phenomena for subsets of closed symplectic manifolds using partial symplectic quasi-states constructed through Hamiltonian Floer theory and quantum homology. These quasi-states assign distinguished values to Hamiltonians and lead to several related notions of rigidity—ranging from nondisplaceability to stronger heavy- and superheavy-type properties. Each level in the hierarchy yields corresponding intersection theorems: sufficiently rigid subsets cannot be displaced by Hamiltonian isotopies, and subsets satisfying complementary rigidity conditions must intersect one another.

The resulting framework applies especially well to Poisson-commutative systems. Given a finite-dimensional Poisson-commutative algebra of smooth functions, or the associated moment map, the quasi-state determines distinguished fibers that exhibit strong intersection properties. The arguments do not require all fibers to be regular or smooth. Consequently, they can detect rigid subsets contained in singular moment-map fibers and, more generally, in possibly singular level sets arising from Poisson-commutative function algebras.

The theory also produces new intersections between such distinguished fibers and monotone Lagrangian submanifolds whose Floer-theoretic invariants do not vanish. Under appropriate hypotheses, a monotone Lagrangian is shown to satisfy one of the rigidity conditions in the hierarchy. It must therefore intersect every subset enjoying the corresponding dual property, including suitable moment-map fibers selected by a partial symplectic quasi-state. This provides a unified Floer-theoretic mechanism for proving intersections that may be inaccessible through transversality, dimension-counting, or classical symplectic-topological arguments alone.

Finally, the intersection results have algebraic consequences. If the quantum homology of the ambient manifold were semisimple, its decomposition into field factors would supply idempotents and associated partial quasi-states with particularly strong properties. The required intersection behavior can conflict with the existence of certain disjoint rigid subsets or with the geometry of monotone Lagrangians and singular integrable-system fibers. Such configurations therefore give geometric obstructions to semisimplicity. In this way, the work links the algebraic structure of quantum homology to concrete intersection patterns in symplectic geometry and broadens the range of subsets whose rigidity can be detected by Floer-theoretic methods.
outputs.L5:
### Hamiltonian and Lagrangian Perspectives in the Work of Peter Albers

Hamiltonian and Lagrangian formalisms are two fundamental approaches to classical mechanics and modern symplectic geometry. The Lagrangian formulation describes a system through a function \(L(q,\dot q,t)\), usually defined as the difference between kinetic and potential energy. Its dynamics are determined by the Euler–Lagrange equations. The Hamiltonian formulation instead uses positions and momenta, with a Hamiltonian function \(H(q,p,t)\) that often represents the system’s total energy. Hamilton’s equations then describe the resulting motion in phase space.

These viewpoints also have important geometric meanings. A Hamiltonian generates a flow on a symplectic manifold, while a Lagrangian submanifold is a subspace on which the symplectic form vanishes and whose dimension is half that of the ambient manifold. Lagrangian submanifolds frequently represent boundary conditions, constraints, or possible configurations of a mechanical system.

Mathematician Peter Albers has contributed to research connecting Hamiltonian dynamics, symplectic topology, contact geometry, and Lagrangian intersection theory. Methods such as Floer homology and variational techniques make it possible to study periodic trajectories, intersections of Lagrangian submanifolds, and other global properties that cannot be detected through local differential equations alone.

In this setting, Hamiltonian and Lagrangian ideas are more than alternative descriptions of mechanics. They provide a geometric framework for investigating the existence and structure of dynamical trajectories. Work by Albers and other researchers demonstrates how this framework links classical physical intuition with sophisticated questions in contemporary geometry and topology.

counterfactuals.output: We study intersection rigidity in closed symplectic manifolds through partial symplectic quasi-states. By associating heaviness-type properties to subsets and exploiting quasi-linearity on Poisson-commuting functions, we derive criteria ensuring that certain families of subsets must have nonempty intersection. The resulting obstruction is invariant under Hamiltonian isotopies and extends classical nondisplaceability phenomena beyond settings where spectral or Floer-theoretic calculations are directly available. Applications include rigidity results for fibers of moment-type maps and configurations of heavy and superheavy subsets.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results and methods of a symplectic geometry paper that establishes a hierarchy of nondisplaceable sets, studies moment-map fibers and monotone Lagrangians, and derives obstructions to semisimplicity of quantum homology.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops a hierarchy of symplectic rigidity for subsets of a closed symplectic manifold, organized through spectral invariants and partial symplectic quasi-states.

### Main results

- **Heavy and superheavy subsets.**  
  Relative to a partial symplectic quasi-state \(\zeta\), a set \(X\) is:
  - **heavy** if \(\zeta(F)\ge \inf_X F\) for every continuous \(F\);
  - **superheavy** if \(\zeta(F)\le \sup_X F\).

  Superheavy sets are heavy; heavy sets are stably nondisplaceable, and every superheavy set must intersect every heavy set associated to the same quasi-state. Thus these notions strengthen ordinary nondisplaceability and provide robust intersection results.

- **Poisson-commutative moment maps and stems.**  
  For a finite-dimensional Poisson-commutative family of Hamiltonians, the paper studies fibers of its moment map. A fiber whose other fibers are displaceable—a **stem**—is shown to be superheavy. More generally, quasi-state methods guarantee distinguished nondisplaceable fibers. This gives a systematic way to detect rigid toric and integrable-system fibers, including special Lagrangian torus fibers.

- **Monotone Lagrangians.**  
  Lagrangian Floer homology is used to show that suitable monotone Lagrangians with nonvanishing Floer-theoretic invariants are heavy, and in stronger situations superheavy, for quasi-states determined by appropriate idempotents in quantum homology. Consequently such Lagrangians are stably nondisplaceable and satisfy strong intersection constraints.

- **Products and hierarchy.**  
  The rigidity notions behave well under products, allowing heavy or superheavy subsets in different manifolds to produce rigid subsets in product manifolds. The paper thereby distinguishes several levels of rigidity that ordinary displacement theory cannot separate.

- **Obstructions to semisimplicity of quantum homology.**  
  If quantum homology were semisimple, its decomposition into field factors would yield a corresponding finite collection of idempotents and spectral quasi-states. Floer-essential Lagrangians would then have to be heavy or superheavy for some factor. Configurations of disjoint Lagrangians can contradict the mandatory intersection of heavy and superheavy sets. This converts symplectic intersection data into an obstruction to semisimplicity of the quantum homology algebra.

### Principal methods

1. **Hamiltonian spectral invariants** associated with idempotents in quantum homology.
2. **Homogenization** of spectral invariants to construct partial symplectic quasi-states and Calabi-type quasi-morphisms.
3. **Vanishing and quasi-linearity properties** on displaceable supports and Poisson-commuting Hamiltonians.
4. **Moment-map localization**, using displaceability of most fibers to force quasi-state mass onto a distinguished fiber.
5. **Lagrangian Floer theory and quantum module/open–closed structures**, relating nonzero Floer classes to ambient quantum-homology idempotents.
6. **Algebraic decomposition arguments**, translating semisimplicity of quantum homology into geometric intersection requirements.

Overall, the paper creates a bridge between spectral/Floer invariants, rigidity of moment-map fibers and monotone Lagrangians, and the algebraic structure of quantum homology.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a single-paragraph mathematical abstract describing new rigidity-of-intersection results for Hamiltonian torus actions, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, and singular sets arising from Poisson-commutative subalgebras.
counterfactuals.output: We establish new rigidity-of-intersection results in symplectic manifolds equipped with Hamiltonian torus actions and, more generally, Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. For a closed monotone Lagrangian submanifold with nonvanishing Floer-theoretic invariants, we identify conditions ensuring that every Hamiltonian image intersects prescribed torus-invariant level sets, including singular fibers of the associated moment-type map. Our results extend classical nondisplaceability phenomena beyond regular moment-map fibers to singular sets determined by rank drops and critical strata of Poisson-commutative systems. The proofs combine equivariant symplectic reduction, monotone Lagrangian Floer theory, and spectral-invariant methods, yielding quantitative intersection bounds in the transverse case and stable nondisplaceability under perturbations of both the integrable system and the Lagrangian. These theorems provide a unified rigidity framework for toric and partially integrable Hamiltonian systems and reveal new constraints on the topology and displacement behavior of their singular fibers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in the style of a journal abstract, how Floer-theoretic partial symplectic quasi-states can be used to compare intersection rigidity properties and obtain geometric consequences for quantum homology.
counterfactuals.output: We describe a Floer-theoretic method for comparing intersection-rigidity phenomena through partial symplectic quasi-states associated with idempotents in quantum homology. Spectral invariants define homogeneous, monotone functionals on Hamiltonians whose restrictions to Poisson-commuting families yield partial quasi-linearity. The corresponding notions of heavy and superheavy subsets convert inequalities between quasi-states into geometric intersection statements: superheavy sets intersect every heavy set for the same quasi-state and are, in particular, Hamiltonianly nondisplaceable. By testing several quasi-states on functions adapted to distinguished subsets—such as Lagrangians, fibers of integrable systems, or skeleta—one can compare their rigidity profiles. A subset heavy for one idempotent but displaceable, or non-heavy, for another separates the associated spectral functionals and hence distinguishes the underlying quantum-homology classes. Conversely, common superheaviness forces robust pairwise intersections and obstructs simultaneous displacement. These comparisons translate geometric configurations into algebraic consequences: nonvanishing or linear independence of idempotents, lower bounds on the rank or semisimple factors of quantum homology, and constraints on quantum products. Thus partial symplectic quasi-states provide a bridge from Floer spectral data to concrete intersection rigidity and, in the reverse direction, use geometric nondisplaceability to detect structure in quantum homology.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an abstract for a symplectic topology article building on Albers and Biran–Cornea, with applications to nondisplaceability, specific moment-map fibers, Poisson-commutative function algebras, and semisimplicity obstructions.
counterfactuals.output: We develop a Floer-theoretic criterion for nondisplaceability that combines Albers’s comparison morphism with the Lagrangian quantum-homological framework of Biran–Cornea. Under suitable monotonicity and unobstructedness assumptions, nonvanishing of the Lagrangian unit—or, more generally, of its image in Hamiltonian Floer homology—forces a Lagrangian submanifold to be nondisplaceable and yields intersection results for pairs detected by compatible quantum idempotents. We apply this criterion to Poisson-commutative systems, showing that their spectra contain distinguished fibers that are nondisplaceable; in particular, we recover and extend nondisplaceability statements for barycentric toric moment-map fibers and selected Gelfand–Cetlin fibers. The resulting construction associates nondisplaceable fibers to idempotent summands of quantum homology and gives rigidity consequences for finite-dimensional Poisson-commutative function algebras. Finally, we prove that sufficiently rich configurations of such fibers obstruct semisimplicity of the relevant quantum homology algebra: the intersection and comparison maps force algebraic relations incompatible with a decomposition into field factors. This provides a unified mechanism linking Lagrangian quantum homology, integrable systems, Poisson-commutative rigidity, and the algebraic structure of quantum homology.
